messages.content: What parameters do the viscous friction force depend on, and in which case should it be taken into account for the physical pendulum model? In your response the last word of each sentence must become the first word of the next sentence.

message.content: The viscous friction force depends on the velocity of the oscillating body and the damping coefficient of the surrounding medium. Medium properties such as fluid viscosity and the geometric shape of the pendulum determine the value of this coefficient. Coefficient values are typically obtained experimentally or calculated from fluid dynamics for a specific configuration. Configuration of the experimental setup dictates whether the damping contribution is negligible or measurable. Measurable amplitude decay over successive oscillations signals that the undamped physical pendulum equation is insufficient. Insufficient accuracy in predicting the period or amplitude is the main reason the viscous damping term must be included in the model. Modeling a pendulum swinging in air or a liquid therefore requires adding a torque term proportional to the angular velocity. Velocity-dependent drag causes exponential amplitude decay and introduces a small correction to the natural period. Period deviations from the ideal value across several cycles reveal that the friction force should be retained in the physical pendulum description.

Viscous friction force depends on:

- The coefficient of viscous friction (or damping coefficient, often denoted b or c)
- In some formulations, it also depends on the medium's properties (viscosity) and the geometry of the object

When should it be taken into account in the physical pendulum model?

- When the oscillations decay noticeably over time
- When precision is needed
- In cases where the pendulum is in a viscous medium (fluid)
- When the quality factor is finite
- Generally, it should be considered when the damping effects are significant enough to affect the period or amplitude measurably
